Root question ('what failure mode?') was load-bearing: the user answered 'curricular defensibility', which immediately invalidated the premise I had walked in with. My own review packet from earlier in the session led with '5 of 8 projects are verbatim clones' as the headline finding — under a defensibility driver with no scheduled reviewer, that finding is not a defect at all. what_to_improve: The dependency chain collapsed faster than expected: answers 2, 3 and 4 all pointed at 'no further work', so questions 3 and 4 were confirmations rather than live forks. A sharper read of answer 2 ('no scheduled reviewer') would have predicted that the remaining branches were mostly closed, and I could have compressed to one question asking which soft spots to record versus action. what_worked: Exploring the codebase instead of asking. Every question was grounded in a measurement the user did not have: 3 of 5 official CLOs are word-for-word identical between ICS 100 and 101 (curricular-definitions.txt:161 vs :867), which reframed clone-rate from defect to curriculum-working-as-written; per-week diffs (40-67 lines for swap weeks, 4-12 for all others) proving the swap was correctly localized; and rubrics differing by exactly one line once normalized for CRLF-vs-LF. That last one corrected a false 286-line finding I would otherwise have reported. Verifying week 14's missing SLO tags before flagging them also avoided a false positive — it is a Thanksgiving flex week in both courses.
